Underwater acoustic metamaterials are artificial periodic structures with microstructures that can create band gaps to suppress sound waves in certain frequency ranges.
Local resonance metamaterials (LRM) use rubber-coated metal spheres embedded in viscoelastic polymers to achieve low-frequency sound absorption between 600 and 2000 Hz.
The average sound absorption coefficient of a particle-filled polyurethane metamaterial plate with spiral resonators is 0.54 in the 0.8–6 kHz range under normal pressure.
The same metamaterial plate maintains an average absorption coefficient of 0.51 in the 1.5–6 kHz range under 0.5 MPa hydrostatic pressure.
Gradient exponential metamaterials with acoustic black hole effects can achieve omnidirectional broadband sound absorption underwater.
Open-cell SiC foam filled with silicone oil improves impedance matching and achieves sound absorption coefficients close to one in the 750–4000 Hz range.
Chiral metamaterials with negative Poisson’s ratio exhibit enhanced vibration isolation and sound insulation below 50 Hz.
Honeycomb-type acoustic metamaterial plates can achieve an average sound transmission loss of 10 dB in the 2–10 kHz range under 3 MPa hydrostatic pressure.
Pentamode metamaterials have shear modulus far less than bulk modulus, enabling anisotropic acoustic wave manipulation and underwater acoustic cloaking.
Pentamode metamaterial cloaks assembled from single-phase solid materials can achieve segmented frequency range stealth but have limited broadband performance.
The narrow bandwidth of local resonance metamaterials can be broadened by coupling multiple resonance units with different frequencies.
Sound insulation decoupling metamaterials (SIDM) reduce near-field self-noise caused by flow-induced vibration to improve sonar detection and stealth.
Traditional porous metamaterials have weak low-frequency vibration suppression and isolation, limiting their decoupling effectiveness.
Negative Poisson’s ratio materials contract longitudinally when compressed and expand longitudinally when stretched, aiding in sound insulation.
Underwater acoustic guided metamaterials (UAGM) steer sound waves to bypass targets, achieving acoustic stealth by controlling wave propagation paths.
Hydrostatic pressure resistance is a critical design factor for underwater acoustic metamaterials to maintain performance in deep-sea environments.
The band gap in phononic crystals is mainly formed by Bragg scattering, requiring large cell sizes for low-frequency control, limiting engineering applications.
Local resonance band gaps arise from resonance effects of embedded units, enabling subwavelength low-frequency sound control.
The impedance mismatch between underwater acoustic equipment and water can cause self-noise transmission, which SIDM aims to block.
The paper emphasizes the need for metamaterials that combine broadband absorption, low frequency operation, and pressure resistance for future underwater acoustic equipment.
